newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia eyes Black Sea ports upgrade with U.S firm.
newsitem.headline: Georgia eyes Black Sea ports upgrade with U.S firm.

text.p: Ex-Soviet Georgia's national oil company and Transoceanic Shipping Company of the United States said on Thursday that they would form a joint venture to expand the capacity of Georgian ports on the Black Sea.
Arval Handrick, vice chairman of Transoceanic, told a news conference the project envisioned upgrading facilities to handle dry cargo traffic expected for big regional energy projects.

"This is a large project which involves the reconstruction of Georgia's ports at Poti and Batumi so that they can be used for bringing in shipments for oil companies in Central Asia and the Caspian Sea area," he told a joint news conference with Gia Chanturia, president of the Georgian International Oil Company.
"The Baku region is virtually locked and the problem is to bring materials into Baku."
Chanturia said the joint venture would work to increase Poti's capacity from six million tonnes per year of dry cargo to 14 million tonnes over the next 18 months.
The port could eventually handle up to 40 million tonnes per year, he said, adding that it could be used to export oil from the Caspian and Central Asia.
"We've made no secret of the fact that we are interested in using Georgia for the transit of Caspian and Central Asian oil," he said.
Chanturia and Handrick both declined to give figures on the amount of money needed for the ugrades or how they would be financed.

Azerbaijan International Operating Co (AIOC), a consortium of western energy firms and Azeri state oil company SOCAR, began importing equipment for its $8 billion project in the Caspian Sea through Georgian ports earlier this year.
Chevron Corp and Mobil Corp have already begun production in Kazakhstan.
AIOC has already said it will use an existing pipeline from Azerbaijan through Georgia for exporting some of its "early oil" output.

AIOC president Terry Adams said last month that Georgia's Batumi outlet was the group's preferred export route for the 700,000-800,000 tonnes of main oil that it will eventually bring on stream, and that Georgia is a leading candidate for the construction of a new pipeline for Caspian oil.
